1.note: Price line sits directly before 'almost everyone in classical music believed these old violins had a special sound'; distractors are unsupported ('few players had ever touched' is contradicted by soloists who played them on stage for years). Fact check (a): Fritz et al. Paris/Indianapolis studies as described (about 20 players, 3 old + 3 new, welder's goggles, dim room, perfume, least-liked a famous old one, 6 of 10 soloists chose new, audience tests) match the published record. Speech (c): natural, contractions throughout.

2.note: Implied by 'a talented young violinist doesn't need a fortune to own an instrument that sounds excellent' against 'several million dollars'. 'Tiny fraction' is stronger wording than the talk uses, but it is loose wording of a point the speaker makes, not a new inference. 'Need years of playing' is contradicted by new violins 'only a few years old' winning.

3.note: Stated directly: 'so nobody could recognise the smell of old wood'. Distractors not in the talk.

4.note: 'Six of the ten chose a new violin' plus 'played these old instruments on stage for years'. Key says the group did not favour old violins, which holds for the majority (4 of 10 may have chosen old; loose but clearly best). All three distractors contradict the talk. Minor gap: 'six of the ten' is the first mention of ten soloists; a note, not a defect.

5.note: Key is the best summary; it omits the 'couldn't tell old from new' and expectation points but no distractor captures those either. 'Sounds richer when players cannot see it', 'soloists hear differences other players miss', 'trained players judge better than audiences' are each unsupported or contradicted.

6.note: Followed by 'They're beautiful instruments, and some players will always love them'. Distractors unrelated (eyes covered, next week's experiment, changed mind).

batch_patterns.evidence: All six items share one lecture, and keys confirm each other across stems: item 5's key 'players preferred new violins to old ones' restates item 4's key 'didn't favour old violins' and directly refutes item 4's distractor 'Most of them picked one of the famous old Italian violins'; item 2's stem 'good new violins' plus item 6's stem quote also signal the talk's pro-new stance. A student answering item 5 gets item 4 for free. Key letters B,C,C,B,D,C (no A, C 3 of 6) is not a significant positional pattern on n=6; key length longest in 3 of 6 (items 2, 3, 5), not a pattern.
